prompt:
In the $8\times 8$ grid below, label 8 squares with X and 8 squares with Y such that:

1. No square can be labeled with both an X and a Y.
2. Each row and each column must contain exactly one square labeled X and one square labeled Y.
3. Any square marked with a $\star$ or a $\heartsuit$ cannot be labeled with an X or a Y.
4. We say that a square marked with a $\star$ or a $\heartsuit$ *sees* a label (X or Y) if one can move in a straight line horizontally or vertically from the marked square to the square with the label, without crossing any other squares with X's or Y's. It is OK to cross other squares marked with a $\star$ or $\heartsuit$. Using this definition:
   (a) Each square marked with a $\star$ must see exactly 2 X's and 1 Y.
   (b) Each square marked with a $\heartsuit$ must see exactly 1 X and 2 Y's.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star & \star & \star & \star & \star & \phantom{X}\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \heartsuit & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \heartsuit\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X}\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X}\\\hline\end{array}$$

There is a unique solution, but you do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible. You merely need to find an answer that satisfies the conditions of the problem.
answer:
The unique solution:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline X & \phantom{X} & \star & \star & \star & \star & \star & Y\\\hline \phantom{X} & Y & X & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & Y & X & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \heartsuit & \phantom{X} & Y & \phantom{X} & X & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & Y & X & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & X & \phantom{X} & Y & \heartsuit\\\hline Y & X & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X}\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & Y & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & X\\\hline\end{array}$$

solutions.title: Start with the long lines of stars
solutions.body:
Number rows and columns $1$–$8$ from the top left. A marked square sees at most one label in each of the four directions (the first label it meets), and marked squares do not block the view.

* **Row 1** has stars in columns 3–7, so its X and Y lie in columns 1, 2 or 8. If both were on the left, each of these stars would see only one label in the row plus at most one below — fewer than 3. So one label is in column 8 and the other in column 1 or 2. Every row-1 star then sees one X and one Y in the row, so **the topmost label in each of columns 3–7 is an X**.
* **Column 8** has stars in rows 2–5 and a heart in row 6, so its two labels are in row 1 and in row 7 or 8. Each of the four stars sees both of them (one X, one Y), so **the rightmost label in each of rows 2–5 is an X**. The heart in row 6 also sees both, so **the rightmost label in row 6 is a Y**.
* The star in row 7, column 5 and the heart in row 4, column 2 then pin down the remaining positions.

Continuing these deductions gives
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline X & \phantom{X} & \star & \star & \star & \star & \star & Y\\\hline \phantom{X} & Y & X & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & Y & X & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \heartsuit & \phantom{X} & Y & \phantom{X} & X & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & Y & X & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & X & \phantom{X} & Y & \heartsuit\\\hline Y & X & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X}\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & Y & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & X\\\hline\end{array}$$

**Check.** Every row and column contains exactly one X and one Y, no marked square is labeled, each of the ten stars sees exactly two X's and one Y, and each of the two hearts sees exactly one X and two Y's. A computer search over all placements confirms the solution is unique.

**Answer: the grid above.**

prompt:
Let $\mathbb{Z}^+$ denote the set of positive integers. Determine, with proof, if there exists a function $f : \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that
$$f(f(f(f(f(n))))) = 2022n$$
for all positive integers $n$.
answer:
**Yes.** E.g. with a prime $p 
mid 2022$ (say $p = 5$) and $v = 
u_p(n)$: $f(n) = pn$ if $v 
ot\equiv 4 \pmod 5$, and $f(n) =  rac{2022\,n}{p^4}$ if $v \equiv 4 \pmod 5$.

solutions.title: Cycle the exponent of a spare prime
solutions.body:
Let $p$ be a prime not dividing $2022 = 2\cdot 3\cdot 337$, e.g. $p = 5$, and let $\nu_p(n)$ be the exponent of $p$ in $n$. Define
$$f(n) = \begin{cases} p\,n & \text{if } \nu_p(n) \not\equiv 4 \pmod 5,\\[2pt] \dfrac{2022\,n}{p^4} & \text{if } \nu_p(n) \equiv 4 \pmod 5.\end{cases}$$
In the second case $\nu_p(n) \ge 4$, so $f(n)$ is a positive integer.

**Effect on the exponent.** In the first case $\nu_p$ increases by 1; in the second case it decreases by 4 (since $p \nmid 2022$). In both cases the residue of $\nu_p$ modulo 5 increases by 1: $0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4 \to 0$.

**Five applications.** Starting from $n$, the residues of $\nu_p$ before each of the five applications run through all five classes mod 5, each exactly once. So exactly one of the five steps (the one starting in class 4) multiplies by $\frac{2022}{p^4}$, and the other four multiply by $p$. Multiplication commutes, so
$$f^{5}(n) = n\cdot p^4\cdot \frac{2022}{p^4} = 2022\,n.$$

So such a function exists. ∎ (Many other functions work too.)

prompt:
A positive integer $N$ is called *googolicious* if there are exactly $10^{100}$ positive integers $x$ that satisfy the equation
$$\left\lfloor \frac{N}{\left\lfloor \frac{N}{x} \right\rfloor} \right\rfloor = x,$$
where $\lfloor z \rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $z$. Find, with proof, all googolicious integers.

solutions.title: Count solutions via $m = \lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$
solutions.body:
Only $1 \le x \le N$ can work (for $x > N$ the inner floor is $0$). For such $x$ write $N = qx + r$ with $q = \lfloor N/x\rfloor \ge 1$ and $0 \le r < x$. Then
$$\left\lfloor \frac{N}{q}\right\rfloor = \left\lfloor x + \frac rq\right\rfloor = x + \left\lfloor \frac rq\right\rfloor,$$
so **$x$ is a solution iff $r < q$**, and then $\lfloor N/q\rfloor = x$.

Let $m = \lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$, so $m^2 \le N < (m+1)^2$.

**Small solutions, $x \le m$.** Then $q = \lfloor N/x\rfloor \ge \lfloor N/m\rfloor \ge m \ge x > r$, so all $m$ values $x = 1, \dots, m$ are solutions.

**Large solutions, $x > m$.** Then $q \le N/x < (m+1)^2/(m+1) = m+1$, so $q \le m$, and $x = \lfloor N/q\rfloor$ is determined by $q$. Conversely, for each $q \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ put $x = \lfloor N/q\rfloor$, $N = qx + r'$ with $r' < q$. Since $x \ge \lfloor N/m\rfloor \ge m \ge q > r'$, we get $\lfloor N/x\rfloor = q$ and $\lfloor N/q\rfloor = x$: $x$ is a solution. So the large solutions correspond to those $q \le m$ with $\lfloor N/q\rfloor > m$. For $q \le m - 1$ we have $N/q \ge \frac{m^2}{m-1} > m + 1$, so these all count; for $q = m$, $\lfloor N/m\rfloor > m$ iff $N \ge m(m+1)$.

**Total.**
$$\#\text{solutions} = \begin{cases} 2m & \text{if } N \ge m(m+1),\\ 2m - 1 & \text{if } N < m(m+1).\end{cases}$$
(A computer check of all $N < 3000$ agrees.)

**Googolicious.** $10^{100}$ is even, so we need $m = 5\cdot 10^{99}$ and $N \ge m(m+1)$, together with $N < (m+1)^2$:
$$25\cdot 10^{198} + 5\cdot 10^{99} \le N \le 25\cdot 10^{198} + 10^{100}.$$
∎

prompt: Let $\omega$ be a circle with center $O$ and radius 10, and let $H$ be a point such that $OH = 6$. A point $P$ is called *snug* if, for all triangles $ABC$ with circumcircle $\omega$ and orthocenter $H$, we have that $P$ lies on $\triangle ABC$ or in the interior of $\triangle ABC$. Find the area of the region consisting of all snug points.

solutions.title: The ellipse with foci $O$ and $H$
solutions.body:
Let $\mathcal E$ be the closed region $\{X : OX + XH \le 10\}$, an ellipse with foci $O, H$ and major axis $10$. We show that the snug points are exactly $\mathcal E$.

**Lemma.** In a triangle $ABC$ with orthocenter $H$, the reflection $A'$ of $H$ in line $BC$ lies on the circumcircle. *Proof.* The triangles here are acute (from $\sin^2A + \sin^2B + \sin^2C = 2 + 2\cos A\cos B\cos C$ and $OH^2 = 9R^2 - (a^2+b^2+c^2)$, $OH < R$ forces $\cos A\cos B\cos C > 0$). With $H$ inside, $\angle BHC = 180^\circ - \angle A$ (in quadrilateral formed by $A$, the feet of two altitudes and $H$), so $\angle BA'C = \angle BHC = 180^\circ - \angle A$ and $A'$ (on the other side of $BC$) lies on the circle. $\square$

**Each side is tangent to $\mathcal E$.** For any point $X$ on line $BC$, $XH = XA'$, so
$$OX + XH = OX + XA' \ge OA' = 10,$$
with equality exactly where segment $OA'$ crosses $BC$. Hence line $BC$ touches $\mathcal E$ but does not enter its interior. Since $\mathcal E$ is convex and contains $O$ (as $0 + 6 < 10$), and $O$ is on the same side of $BC$ as $A$ (acute triangle), $\mathcal E$ lies in the closed half-plane of $BC$ containing $A$. The same holds for the other two sides, so $\mathcal E \subseteq \triangle ABC$ for every such triangle: **all points of $\mathcal E$ are snug**.

**Nothing else is snug.** Let $Q \notin \mathcal E$ and let ray $OQ$ meet the boundary of $\mathcal E$ at $T$. Let $t$ be the tangent line to $\mathcal E$ at $T$ and $A'$ the reflection of $H$ in $t$; by the reflection property of the ellipse, $O, T, A'$ are collinear and $OA' = OT + TH = 10$, so $A' \in \omega$. Line $t$ passes through $T$, which is inside $\omega$, so it meets $\omega$ at two points $B, C$; let line $A'H$ meet $\omega$ again at $A$. The altitude from $A$ is line $AA'$ (perpendicular to $t = BC$), and the orthocenter is the point on it whose reflection in $BC$ lies on $\omega$, namely $H$. So $ABC$ is an admissible triangle, its side $BC$ separates $O$ from $Q$ (the segment $OQ$ crosses $t$ at $T$ and $Q$ lies beyond it), and $Q$ is outside $\triangle ABC$: not snug.

**Area.** The ellipse has $2a = 10$, focal distance $2c = 6$, so $a = 5$, $c = 3$, $b = \sqrt{25 - 9} = 4$, and area $\pi ab = 20\pi$.

**Answer: $20\pi$**

prompt: A lattice point is a point on the coordinate plane with integer coordinates. Prove or disprove: there exists a finite set $S$ of lattice points such that for every line $\ell$ in the plane with slope $0$, $1$, $-1$, or undefined, either $\ell$ and $S$ intersect at exactly 2022 points, or they do not intersect.
answer: **True (such $S$ exists).** With $k = 2022$, take $S = \{(a + kb + 2k^2c,\ -a + kb + 2k^3d) : 0 \le a, b, c, d < k\}$; each of the four line directions fixes three of $a, b, c, d$ and leaves the fourth free.

solutions.title: A four-parameter construction
solutions.body:
Let $k = 2022$ (any $k \ge 1$ works) and
$$S = \{(a + kb + 2k^2c,\ \ -a + kb + 2k^3d) : a, b, c, d \in \{0, 1, \dots, k-1\}\}.$$

**Two facts.** (i) The numbers $a + kb$ take each value in $[0, k^2)$ exactly once (base-$k$ digits). (ii) The numbers $kb - a$ take each value in $[-(k-1), k^2 - k]$ exactly once — $k^2$ consecutive integers — so they are distinct modulo $k^2$.

**The points are distinct.** Since $x = (a + kb) + 2k^2c$ with $0 \le a + kb < k^2$, the value of $x$ determines $c$ (quotient by $2k^2$) and $a + kb$ (remainder), hence $(a, b, c)$ by fact (i); then $y$ determines $d$. So $|S| = k^4$.

For each line, we show the intersection points are obtained by fixing three of the parameters uniquely and letting the fourth run freely over its $k$ values; hence each line meets $S$ in $0$ or exactly $k$ points.

* **Vertical, $x = n$:** $(a + kb) + 2k^2 c = n$ determines $(a, b, c)$ (if a solution exists); $d$ is free.
* **Horizontal, $y = n$:** $(kb - a) + 2k^3 d = n$. Modulo $k^2$ this fixes $kb - a$ by fact (ii), hence $(a, b)$, and then $d$; $c$ is free.
* **Slope 1, $x - y = n$:** $x - y = 2(a + k^2 c - k^3 d)$. The number $a + k^2c$ lies in $[0, k^3)$ and is determined by $n/2 \bmod k^3$; it determines $(a, c)$ (digits), and then $d$. $b$ is free.
* **Slope $-1$, $x + y = n$:** $x + y = 2k(b + kc + k^2 d)$, and $b + kc + k^2d$ determines $(b, c, d)$ (base-$k$ digits). $a$ is free.

So every such line meets $S$ in either no points or exactly $k = 2022$ points. (A computer check confirms the construction for $k = 3, 4, 5$.) ∎
